content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review:
This paper presents a new adaptive curriculum learning loss (CurricularFace) that embeds the idea of curriculum learning into the loss function to achieve a novel training strategy for deep face recognition, which mainly addresses easy samples in the early training stage and hard ones in the later stage. Experimental results on LFW, CFP-FP, CPLFW, AgeDB, CALFW, IJB-B, IJB-C, and MegaFace verified the efficacy of the proposed method.

The writing is clear and the presentation is satisfactory.

My concerns regarding this paper are as below.
1) What is the training computational complexity and testing time cost compared with previous works, e.g., ArcFace [Deng et al., CVPR 2019], Enforced Cross-Entropy [Zhao et al., CVPR 2018]?
2) When perform evaluations on IJB-B/C, did the authors adopt specific strategies for set-based face recognition? What are the quantitative  comparisons between the proposed CurricularFace and NAN [Yang et al., CVPR 2017], MPNet [Zhao et al., IJCAI 2019]?
3) Does the proposed CurricularFace only work on face? Can it generalize to other tasks? e.g., detection, segmentation.
4) Any theoretical analysis on the choice of scale s and margin m?

Based on the above comments, I decide to give the initial rate of Weak Reject for this paper, if the authors could solve my concerns in rebuttal, I would like to further adjust my rate.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #1
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, and we correspondingly address the reviewer's concerns as follows.

R1Q1). Training time Complexity.
The proposed method only brings small burden on training complexity, but has the same cost as the backbone model during inference. Specifically, compared with the conventional margin-based loss functions, our loss only additionally adjusts the negative cosine similarity of hard samples. Under the same environment and batchsize, ArcFace~\cite{deng2018arcface} costs $0.102$s for each iteration on $4$ NVIDIA M$40$ GPUs, while ours costs $0.126$s.

R1Q1). Testing on IJB-B and IJB-C.
As described in paragraph "Results on IJB-B and IJB-C” of our submission, we follow the same testing protocol in ArcFace~\cite{deng2018arcface} and DO not adopt any specific strategies for set-based face recognition. Note that our method is not proposed for set-based face recognition task, and the experiments on these two datasets are just to prove that our loss can obtain more discriminate features than the baselines like ArcFace, which are also generic methods for face recognition. Last but not least, although NAN is proposed for set-based face recognition, our method still achieves better TAR performance than the reported results in NAN on IJB-A dataset ($97.3$ over~$94.1$ @FAR=$0.01$). 

R1Q3). Other tasks.
Thanks for your suggestion. The proposed method mainly focuses on the open-set face recognition, and achieves SOTA performance on various kinds of popular facial benchmarks. Generalizing the proposed loss to other tasks, such as person Re-Identification and fine-grained classification, may be a good direction for further study.

R1Q4). Theoretical analysis on the choice of scale $s$ and margin $m$.
In fact, the introduction of these two hyper-parameters is not the contribution of our method. 
We just follow ArcFace~\cite{deng2018arcface} to set the values of scale $s$ and margin $m$.  Please refer to the previous margin-based loss functions~\cite{liu2017sphereface,wang2018cosface,deng2018arcface} for more details.

[deng2018arcface]: Jiankang  Deng,   Jia  Guo,   and  Stefanos  Zafeiriou. Arc-face: Additive angular margin loss for deep face recognition. In CVPR, 2019.
[liu2017sphereface]: Weiyang  Li,  Yandong  Wen,  Zhiding  Yu,  Ming  Li,  BhikshaRaj, and Le Song.  Sphereface: Deep hypersphere embeddingfor face recognition. In CVPR, 2017.
[wang2018cosface] Hao Wang, Yitong Wang, Zheng Zhou, Xing Ji, Dihong Gong,Jingchao Zhou, Zhifeng Li, and Wei Liu. Cosface: Large mar-gin cosine loss for deep face recognition. In CVPR, 2018.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
The paper proposes a curriculum learning strategy for face recognition and verification learning. The proposed strategy adaptively modulates the weight of the wrongly classified samples throughout the training.  The modulation coefficient used is directly linearly dependent  on the average similarity of the positive samples (that is pairs of features belonging to the same face class in the training triplets). The average similarity is computed with momentum 0.99 across training batches. It is logical to expect that this modulation factor is small at the early stages of training as the backbone has not yet learned a good feature representation that would result in high correct similarity, yet near the end of training the positive similarity increases, and the hard examples get to be modulated with higher coefficient. The proposed training strategy is evaluated on numerous benchmarks and demonstrates consistent improvements in the range of 0.02% to 0.6% accuracy. Some claims on the improved stability of the proposed approach are made.

Although I am not an expert on most recent face recognition techniques, I feel this paper drives an interesting point and has a useful contribution to the community. Therefore I recommend acceptance. However, I urge the authors to consider improving a few points:

1. there is a certain discussion on why focal loss is not a valid choice for a curriculum learning strategy. I feel I am not entirely convinced, and I suggest the authors to simple run the comparative experiments on all of their tests.

2. Some notations used are not so well explained and some are introduced only after already being used, I suggest to improve that. In particular the N(.) and the I(.) and the angles that appear without proper definition (it is possible to understand from the context, but I would not burden the reader).

3. I feel like more ablation studies could be done on the design choices of the modulation function.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #3
content.comment:
Thanks for your valuable comments, and we correspondingly address the reviewer's concerns as follows.

R3Q1). Comparison with Focal Loss.
Actually, the previous work~\cite{wang2018sv} already compared their proposed SV-Arc-Softmax with Focal loss on two representative benchmarks: LFW and MegaFace (Id.: Rank-1@1e-6, Ver.: TPR@FAR=1e-6, and 'R' denotes data refinement on both probe set and 1M distractors) with the same training data and the same backbone. The results are as follows, and our method consistently outperforms SV-Arc-Softmax and Focal loss on all of the cases.

Methods (\%)     |     LFW    | MegaFace (Id., R) | MegaFace (Ver., R) 
Focal                    |  $99.66$ |        $94.47$           |         $94.84$          
SV-Arc-Softmax  | $99.78$  |       $97.20$           |          $97.38$ 
Ours                     |  $99.80$ |       $98.71$           |          $98.64$   

R3Q2). Notations definition (I($\cdot$) and N($\cdot$)).
In our revision, we will introduce the definitions of the notations of I and N before we use it.

R3Q3). The choice of the modulation function.
Thanks for your good question. Unfortunately, the proposed function in our submission is the ONLY solution that we have figured out. But as described in the ``conclusion'' of our submission, designing a better modulation function for negative cosine similarity that shares similar adaptive characteristic during training may be a good direction as the future work.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
This paper presents a method for training a facial recognition system, CurricularFace, that creates adaptive loss functions that is both "margin-based" and is adaptive over time, increasing emphasis on harder examples and decreasing emphasis on easier examples over time.  The experimental results seem compelling, but I am not very familiar with the area, so it is difficult for me to judge.

 It seems like the experimental results are quite good, but I unfortunately can't recommend this paper for acceptance since I found it too difficult to read.   A lot of background seems to be assumed that I don't have and wasn't really provided in the paper 

Here are questions and comments I have that I hope can be worked into the final version:

- From the citations, this seems to be a settled issue in the face recognition field, but why create a margin-based loss function by modifying the softmax in these ways, rather than using a more direct margin-based loss function, such as the various multiclass variants of the hinge loss, where you can set the target margin at per-example level?
- Presentation challenge: The introduction speaks of so many things without definition: "Triplet loss", "semi-hard or hard samples", "mining-based loss functions", "small backbones", the "manually defined constant t" (before any mention of t).  Then in the Related Work section, reference to the "open-set face recognition problem" is not defined. 
- Do you compare any examples that don't take G(p(x))=1?  If not... maybe drop that factor.
- You speak of various "training stages" -- how exactly is the training stage defined?  When do we progress from one stage to the next?  I don't see this in Algorithm 1.

content.title: Response to Reviewer #2
content.comment:
Thanks for your comments, and we correspondingly address the reviewer's concerns as follows.

R2Q1). Margin-based loss function vs multiclass variants of the hinge loss.
A: Previous work~\cite{liu2016large} demonstrated that the margin-based variant of softmax is better than the multiclass variants of hinge loss to obtain more discriminate features, which are critical for a variety of visual classification and verification tasks. Please refer to~\cite{liu2016large} for more experimental results.

R2Q2). Presentation challenge.
A: "``Triplet loss" is a very common metric learning method~\cite{schroff2015facenet}.  
The definition of ``Semi-hard or hard samples" can also be found in~\cite{schroff2015facenet}.  ``
"Small backbones" means small network structures like MobileFaceNet~\cite{chen2018mobilefacenets} compared to ResNet$100$~\cite{he2016deep}. 
Besides, all of the face recognition methods mentioned in our ``"Related Work'' section belong to the open-set face recognition settings~\cite{liu2017sphereface}, which means that the testing identities are usually disjoint from the training set. Actually, these technical terms are widely used in previous face recognition methods~\cite{schroff2015facenet,deng2018arcface}. 
Finally, the definition of the factor $t$ will be introduced before we use it. 
We will polish the above problems in our revision.

R2Q3). The factor G(p(x)).
A: The factor G(p(x)) in Eq.~$3$ is to make it clear when comparing with Focal loss.

R2Q4). The definition of training stages.
A: Basically, $t$ determines the training stages.  When $t+\cos\theta_{j} < 1$, the relative weight of mis-classified samples in mini-batch is reduced, which indicates the early training stage; while when $t+\cos \theta_{j} > 1$, these mis-classified samples are emphasized, which indicates the later training stage. 

[deng2018arcface]: Jiankang  Deng,   Jia  Guo,   and  Stefanos  Zafeiriou. Arc-face: Additive angular margin loss for deep face recognition. In CVPR, 2019.
[he2016deep]: Kaiming He,  Xiangyu Zhang,  Shaoqing Ren,  and Jian Sun. Deep residual learning for image recognition. In CVPR, 2016.
[liu2017sphereface]: Weiyang  Li,  Yandong  Wen,  Zhiding  Yu,  Ming  Li,  BhikshaRaj, and Le Song.  Sphereface: Deep hypersphere embeddingfor face recognition. In CVPR, 2017.
[liu2016large]: Weiyang  Liu,  Yandong  Wen,  Zhiding  Yu,  and  Meng  Yang. Large-margin softmax loss for convolutional neural networks. In ICML, 2016.
[schroff2015facenet]: Florian  Schroff,  Dmitry  Kalenichenko,  and  James  Philbin.Facenet:  A unified embedding for face recognition and clus-tering. In CVPR, 2015.
